 5           1.      Plaintiff Brian Calvert (“Plaintiff”), on behalf of himself and all others similarly situated,

 6   asserts the following against Defendant Meta Platforms, Inc. f/k/a Facebook, Inc. (“Meta”), based upon

 7   personal knowledge, where applicable, information and belief, and the investigation of counsel.

 8                                          NATURE OF THE ACTION

 9           2.      In 2004, Mark Zuckerberg launched TheFacebook.com as a directory and social network

10   for Harvard students. 1 Facebook, now Meta, has since grown, becoming one of the world's largest

11   advertising companies.

12           3.      According to Meta’s Annual 10-K, “[c]urrently, we generate substantially all of our

13   revenue from selling advertising placements on our family of apps to marketers.” 2

14           4.      To operate its advertising business, Meta relies on the tracking tool “Meta Pixel.”

15           5.      Meta Pixel is a snippet of JavaScript code embedded on a third-party website that tracks

16   users’ actions as they navigate through the website. It logs the pages they visit, the buttons they click,

17   the information they type, and more. 3 Meta Pixel then sends this harvested information to Meta, where it

18   can be stored for years. 4

19           6.      The Meta Pixel is marketed towards third parties that use Facebook Ads as a way to

20   “make sure [their] ads are shown to the right people.” Meta boasts that Meta Pixel allows third parties to

 1   improve users’ experiences on their websites, target advertisements more effectively, and drive more

 3              7.    These benefits appeal to third-party websites; 30% of the 100,000 most popular websites

 4   use Meta Pixel, and Meta has reported that millions of iterations of its Pixel are on websites across the

 5   Internet. 6

 6              8.    Recently, it was discovered that Meta was unlawfully monitoring Android smartphone

 7   users’ web traffic. When an Android user accessed either the Facebook or Instagram applications on

 8   their phone, then eventually placed the application into the background, the application would begin

 9   listening for communications recorded, intercepted, redirected, and transmitted via the Meta Pixel. 7

10              9.    The Meta Pixel recorded, transmitted, and exploited event-level data about the user’s

11   interaction with websites. Event-level data tracking includes but is not limited to tracking when a user

12   adds payment information, adds an item to their cart, schedules an appointment, subscribes, views

13   content, searches, and communicates with a representative of the website. 8

14              10.   When a user accessed a website with the Meta Pixel embedded, the Meta Pixel would

15   send the harvested data to the Facebook or Instagram application (“Native Applications”) running in the

16   background of the Android phone to link the consumer’s web activity to their Instagram or Facebook

17   account. 9

18              11.   Plaintiff and Class members are users of Android phones who also had the Facebook and

19   Instagram applications on their devices.

20              12.   By harvesting and transmitting user web browsing data back to native applications, Meta

21   was able to deanonymize the web browsing of Android users, such as the Plaintiff and Class members.

 1   Meta deanonymized the harvested data by linking users' web browsing activity to their Instagram and

 2   Facebook accounts. By linking Plaintiff’s and Class members’ web browsing data with their Facebook

 3   and Instagram accounts, Meta was making its targeted advertising product more valuable but doing so at

 4   the expense of the privacy of Plaintiff and Class members.

 5          13.     Meta monetizes the information it receives through Meta Pixel by using it to generate

 6   highly profitable targeted advertising, the type of advertising on which Meta relies for the majority of its

 7   revenue. 10

 8          14.     The targeted advertising Meta offers for sale includes the ability to target users based on

 9   specific personal information. Meta Pixel did this with Android users through bypassing normal security

10   and privacy protection tools. 11 Meta accomplished this data harvesting and eavesdropping by concealing

11   how the Meta Pixel and the native applications were communicating. 12

12          15.     Defendant’s actions constitute an extreme invasion of Plaintiff’s and Class members’

13   right to privacy and violate federal and state statutory and common law.

14          16.     Plaintiff and Class Members seek legal and equitable relief.

19   smartphone, which runs on the Android operating system.

20          20.     Defendant Meta Platforms, Inc. is a publicly traded corporation, incorporated in the state

21   of Delaware, with a principal place of business at 1 Meta Way, Menlo Park, CA 94025. Meta has users

22   and does business around the world, and throughout the individual states, territories, and

23   commonwealths of the United States.

 1                                           JURISDICTION AND VENUE

 2           21.        This Court has subject matter jurisdiction over this action pursuant to 28 U.S.C §

 3   1332(d), because the amount in controversy for the Class exceeds $5,000,000 exclusive of interest and

 4   costs, there are more than 100 putative class members defined below, and minimal diversity exists

 5   because a significant portion of putative class members are citizens of a state different from the

 6   citizenship of at least one Defendant.

 7           22.        This Court also has subject matter jurisdiction over this action pursuant to 28 U.S.C. §

 8   1331 since this suit is brought under the laws of the United States.

 9           23.        This Court has supplemental jurisdiction over the remaining state law claims pursuant to

10   28 U.S.C. § 1367 because the state law claims form part of the same case or controversy under Article

11   III of the United States Constitution.

12           24.        This Court has general personal jurisdiction over defendant Meta, because Meta’s

13   headquarters are in California, making Meta essentially at home there. The Court’s exercise of personal

14   jurisdiction over defendant Meta would not offend traditional notions of fair play and justice under the

15   Due Process Clause.

16           25.        Venue is proper in this District pursuant to 28 U.S.C. § 1391, as defendant Meta is

17   subject to personal jurisdiction in this district as if it were a separate state.

21   Harvard students compared two students’ photos and voted on who was “hotter,” Mark Zuckerberg

22   began writing code for a new website. 13 This new website would later come to be known as Facebook.

23           27.        Facebook was launched in 2004 and reached its millionth registered user before the

24   year’s end. Merely four years later, Facebook had already reached the milestone of 100 million monthly

25   active users. 14

 3          32.     In 2015, Meta Pixel was announced as a tool to refine Meta’s targeted advertising.

 4          33.     The Meta Pixel is a mechanism that loads JavaScript code which collects detailed and

 5   granular data for every interaction on a page. 22

 6          34.     Once a third-party company, advertiser, or other entity sets up Meta Pixel on a website,

 7   the information collecting and sharing begins.

 8          35.     Importantly, Meta designed Meta Pixel such that Meta receives the information about a

 9   website user’s actions contemporaneously with those actions. This means that as soon as a website user

10   takes any action on a webpage that includes Meta Pixel, it redirects the user’s communications to Meta

11   while the exchange of the communication between the website users and the website is still occurring.

12          36.     In response to congressional questioning in 2018, Meta stated that the Meta Pixel

13   “provide[s] information about users’ activities off Facebook—including information about their device,

14   websites they visit, purchases they make, the ads they see, and how they use their services—whether or

15   not they have a Facebook account or are logged into Facebook.” 23

16          37.     Meta Pixel allows third parties to create a library which logs every time a website visitor

17   takes an action (an “event”) that the third party wants to track (a “conversion”). All of these tracked

18   conversions are then stored so that the third party can analyze the data collected. 24

 1          38.     There are currently more than six million websites using Meta Pixel. 25 On each of those

 2   websites, Meta Pixel collects and sends information to Meta via scripts running in a person’s internet

 3   browser. That data is then delivered to Meta in “data packets” labeled with personally identifiable

 4   information (“PII”), including the user’s IP address.

 5          39.     If a person is logged in to Facebook when they visit a website where Meta Pixel is

 6   installed, Meta is able to link collected data to specific Facebook accounts.

 7          40.     If a person is not logged into Facebook at the time, Meta uses personal information that a

 8   user enters in form fields to match them to their Facebook and/or Instagram profile through a process

 9   called Advanced Matching. With this process, Meta collects emails, first and last names, phone

10   numbers, birthdates, and addresses, then uses that information to connect event tracking data to a

11   specific Facebook profile.

12          41.     Even if a person does not have a Facebook account, has never registered for an account,

13   has never so much as looked at a Facebook or Meta privacy policy, and has no intention to ever join any

14   social media at all, Meta still collects data on that person. When asked by Congress about this

15   maintenance of “shadow profiles” with data of nonusers of Facebook, Mark Zuckerberg responded,

16   “[W]e collect data on people who have not signed up for Facebook for security purposes.” 26

17          42.     Illustrative that Meta has no real controls on data use an collection was in an

18   investigation by The Markup found that Meta Pixel is embedded on the websites of 33 of Newsweek’s

19   top 100 hospitals in the United States. 27 The Markup’s investigation revealed that Meta Pixels installed

20   on hospitals’ websites have been collecting patients’ sensitive health information—“including details

21   about their medical conditions, prescriptions, and doctor’s appointments”—and sending it to Meta. 28

22   This packet of data collected by Meta Pixel is connected to a patient’s IP address, providing Meta with

 3        B. Meta was lurking in the background to eavesdrop on Android Users

 4           43.     Meta used its native applications, running in the background of Android phones, to

 5   bridge the divide between the data collected by Meta Pixel on a website and assigning that data to a

 6   Meta advertising profile. This scheme allowed Meta to exploit the information they gleaned by

 7   eavesdropping to place users into more specific advertising groups.

 8           44.     “This web-to-app ID sharing method bypasses typical privacy protections such as

 9   clearing cookies, Incognito Mode and Android’s permission controls.” 30

10           45.     Android users would download and install the Facebook and/or Instagram applications

11   from the Google Play Store. 31

12           46.     Users of the application are required to provide Meta login credentials to use the

13   functionality of the Instagram or Facebook applications. 32

14           47.     When a user placed the Instagram or Facebook applications into the background, those

15   applications would begin to monitor UDP Ports 12580–12585. The applications were monitoring for the

16   data being transmitted by the Meta Pixel. 33

17           48.     When a user opened their browser and navigated to a website that had the Meta Pixel

18   script, the Meta Pixel would then send the information collected to the native application running in the

19   background, where, if the user was logged into the application, the data would be attached to their Meta

20   advertising profile. 34

21           49.     When a website was accessed through an Android mobile web browser, the Meta Pixel

22   would transmit the data using WebTRC to UDP ports 12580–12585 to any app on the device that is

23   listening on those ports.

 1           51.     Unlike other cookies that are visible through a typical developer view, the process

 2   described here was not visible. 36 The method in which Meta was exploiting Android users was not

 4   websites. 37 Meta took steps to ensure that this process was buried and visible only to itself, and

 5   researchers with special training who were specifically looking for this type of security vulnerability. 38

 6        C. Meta Violated the Android Terms & the Norms of Application Development

 7           52.     Android applications are “Sandboxed.” Sandboxing “isolates apps from each other and

 8   protects apps and the system from malicious apps. 39 “By default, apps can’t interact with each other and

 9   have limited access to the OS. If app A tries to do something malicious, such as read app B’s data or dial

10   the phone without permissions, it’s prevented from doing so because it doesn’t have the appropriate

11   default user privileges.” 40

12           53.     “You run everything in a sandbox, and there is no interaction within different elements

13   running on it. What this attack vector allows is to break the sandbox that exists between the mobile

14   context and the web context. The channel that exists allowed the Android system to communicate what

15   happens in the browser with the identity running in the mobile app.” 41 Here, the way Meta was tracking

16   users and violating their privacy, was by breaking out of the Sandbox. 42

17           54.     Google Chrome offers users the opportunity to browse the web in “incognito mode.” 43

18           55.     Browsing in “incognito mode” allows a user to browse the internet with more privacy

 5         D. Plaintiff’s Factual Allegations
